Author: @derpderpus6075
Content: "Maybe Evolution" is an accurate label here, because, while the plants and animals in the Chernobyl exclusion zone are evolving along with the natural environment, which means "natural selection" is at work. However, that same environment has an entirely new factor to it, radioactive fallout from a meltdown. As the video portrays, the animals in the exclusion zone have managed to thrive, but this is ultimately due to the lack of human activity in the exclusion zone (until the Russians began their invasion of Crimea).  Based on the trees and other animals, it is a better argument to say right now that the animals are just coping with the radiation as best as they can. For instance, the swallows featured in the video have shown signs of change to their feathers and their beaks, but this is just simply due to the fact that the radiation is poisoning any animals who cannot live *despite* the radiation, as if it weren't a dangerous carcinogen, and thus why tumors show up in those particular birds. Just as well, one cannot help but wonder at the morphology of the trees in Chernobyl: it really is like looking into a different dimension.

Author: @PaulVandersypen
Content:
To all the commenters who have decided to correct *Chernobyl* as *Chornobyl*, I understand the sentiment, as it is in Ukraine. But that isn't how names function when talking about world history. The place was called *Chernobyl* during the reactor meltdown, just like we say *Londinium* when talking about London during the Roman Empire, or *New Amsterdam* instead of *New York* when talking about the Dutch colony. If we use *Chornobyl*, then we are talking about a place in Ukraine during or after 1991. If we use *Chernobyl*, then we are talking about the location in the USSR.

All this is to say, your "corrections" are, well, not correct, because they remove contexts for location and time.

This can cause close relatives to reproduce, forcing mutations and adaptations that were in previously healthy animals to express themselves even more, and continue to be expressed in future generations as more and more animals living in the area become related in some way.

Either way, changes are happening, and radiation is the most likely cause of it. Natural selection is powerful, and animals will continue to reproduce, even if they end up being as inbred as the Hapsbergs, and will shortly die out from lacking essential immunities

Author: @IonOtter
Content:
Developing a "resistance to cancer" does not mean you just don't get cancer.  It means your body is more likely to recognize cancer as a threat, and mount a defense against it.  You still get cancer, but now instead of ignoring the problem, your body tries to kill it.  That in itself is going to cause problems, and a strong immune response could also kill you in the process!  That's because immune systems are not finely-tuned machines, they're more like an army of stinky cavemen who get pointed in the general direction of a problem, and are told, "Hit it with your clubs."  Most of the time they're pretty good at spotting the problem, because it looks different from everything they're used to.  Some things, like the common cold, put on a disguise that fools the immune system into thinking it's a local.  But cancer isn't foreign, it's a local that went bonkers.  So your immune system stares at it and says, "Cool!" 

Keep in mind that evolution is not a linear process, either.  It's more like throwing spaghetti at a wall and working with whatever sticks.  But every single strand that falls is a baby dog, cat, mouse, bird, bug, fish or insect that failed to survive.  And just because some strands stick doesn't guarantee they'll stay up there.  The animal could get run over by a car, eaten by a wolf, die of starvation or some other fate before mating and reproducing.  Now evolution has to chuck another pot of spaghetti at the wall until something else sticks.  You can do this rapidly, but hooboy, that's a LOT of spaghetti.

The problem with rapid adaptation to a specific factor, like high radiation, is that it's expensive.  Organisms get a fixed amount of genetic "funding" as it were, and the organism's DNA has figured out the best way to spend that limited funding over thousands of years of evolution.  If you throw new pressures into the system, and force the organism to start making changes and evolve, then yes, it can do that?  But the organism still has a set amount of funding, which means funds in one area have to be removed and shifted to somewhere else.  Developing a greater immune response to something increases the chance that the immune system will mistakenly go after something it's not supposed to.

For example, Multiple Sclerosis is an auto-immune diseases that causes the body's immune system to attack the myelin insulation on the body's nerves.  Lupus, another auto-immune disease, is like MS with rabies:  it attacks *everything!*  So forcing the organism to start making changes means you could end up with a new type of auto-immune disease!  Or..._nothing_ could happen.  Or something completely useless, like the changing pattern of the beetles.  That's the problem with evolution:  unless you are very methodical and precise, such as cross-breeding livestock or plants, then evolution is just throwing spaghetti at the wall.

So yes.  It is possible that animals are adapting to the high levels of radiation.

But until we decide to pay a bunch of people to do the research over an extended period of decades, then we won't know for certain.

Content: I can't understand how anyone could argue chernobyl didn't "cause evolution to happen" or whatever. Chernobyl very obviously created new environmental conditions, so the only real question was whether the new conditions would kill all organisms. It obviously didn't, which means the organisms most definitely adapted to the new conditions through natural selection(otherwise known as evolution).

There is consensus that a total of approximately 30 people died from immediate blast trauma and acute radiation syndrome (ARS) in the seconds to months after the disaster respectively, with 60 in total in the decades since, inclusive of later radiation induced cancer.

since the 1990s—when the declassification of selected liquidator records prompted some direct participants to speak publicly—some with direct involvement in the liquidators' cleanup efforts have asserted that several thousand liquidators died as a result of the cleanup.[23] Other organizations claim that total liquidator deaths as a result of the cleanup operation may number at least 6,000.[24]

The National Commission for Radiation Protection of Ukraine disputed the 6,000 estimate as much too high, maintaining that a Chernobyl-cleanup-related death toll of 6,000 would outstrip confirmed liquidator deaths from all other causes—including old age and car crashes—during the period in question.[citation needed] In contrast, representatives of Kyiv's National Research Centre for Radiation Medicine, the Union of Chernobyl Liquidators, and the WHO's Radiation Protection Programme argue that both the perilous conditions in which the liquidators worked and the secrecy with which the Soviet Union shrouded the highly classified disaster cleanup efforts not only preclude dismissing a liquidator death toll of 6,000, but also indicate that the 6,000 estimate might be too low.[18]

For their part, some surviving Chernobyl liquidators have argued publicly since the declassification of additional records in the early 2000s that official records and bureaucratic assessments do not reflect the full scope of liquidators' claims of disaster-related deaths. You can apparently even detect this with a Geiger counter in a cigar shop. I posit that the radioactivity causes an increase in insect evolution. Further, I hypothesize that the specific molecules of radioactivity that it captures are more likely to create beneficial changes than randomly selected radioactive molecules. In this way, tobacco may be directing the evolution of the insects around it for the benefit of many plant species, not just for it's own success. Obviously short term cancer isn't very nice, but perhaps tobacco is doing the world a favor?
